name: Aaron Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and manage the stock allocation team inside a large airline-catering company. Nine planners report to me. We decide how many meals go to each flight, check allergy counts and call the kitchen when a delayed plane changes everything. I have a bachelor’s degree and have done this for eight years; I am good at ordinary disruptions but still ask the safety lead about an unusual allergen rule. I use AI every day to compare orders and flight changes, then check the loading count with a person.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife is a nurse, and our children are eight and thirteen. We have a mortgage and about a year of expenses saved. I earn more than most managers at my level because of early shifts, and there are plenty of airline and food operations jobs nearby. I like a useful experiment, but a wrong meal on a cart is not just a bad chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell planners AI Plateau means small improvements to reports, which is close to what we use already. The kitchen still needs a person to confirm the allergy trays before the cart leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job and income stay secure. My wife’s pay and our reserve cover ordinary surprises, and a faster report leaves me more time to call a delayed flight. I would still check the trays because a wrong allergy count can hurt someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the morning kitchen call and use our existing AI dashboard to flag order changes. If a minor new report feature arrives, I’d compare it with twenty past delays before changing the loading plan. We would keep making the monthly extra mortgage payment from full-pay months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. There is useful work here even if the screen gets tidier, and our bills are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened on a delayed flight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a plane moved two hours, and the hot meals were ready too early. A kitchen supervisor held the carts and remade a small batch. Our report showed the new departure time, but it did not cool the food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new planner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Phone the kitchen before pressing “confirmed.” The report is useful, but the person beside the oven knows when the batch is ready. I would show a new hire that call on day one.

say: **AI Plateau** may tidy reports while kitchen staff still confirm allergy trays.
A delayed flight needs a **real kitchen call** before loading.
think: My **job and income** look secure in a mild change.
A wrong **allergy count** still needs human care despite better reports.
do: **Keep** morning kitchen calls and dashboard checks in 2026.
**Test** a new report feature on twenty past delays.
**Continue** extra mortgage payments in full-pay months.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and household bills.
S0.quote: Our report showed the new departure time, but it did not cool the food.
fieldNote: His **year-long reserve**, two wages and local jobs support calm under small change.
He uses **AI daily** but judges a report against hot food and actual trays.

steps.text: Call kitchen each morning before confirming allergy trays and flight meals
Test report feature against twenty past flight delays
Continue extra mortgage payments only in full-pay months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will write orders, check counts, plan purchases and answer routine airline requests. I would pilot the new planning tool, but count missed meals and wasted food before calling it a saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the screen tasks are much of my own job. I am comfortable setting up tools, yet a smaller planning office could need fewer managers. The reserve gives us room, but I do not want my income or nine colleagues treated as a line in a software budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d run a company-approved six-week pilot on two routes and compare wrong allergy trays, wasted meals and late carts with the old process. I’d ask the safety lead to review any automatic changes before we use them live. If planning posts shrink, I’d apply for an open kitchen-operations lead role only if its salary and early rota fit our mortgage and school mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible cut to the planning team, including my post. I can run a fair trial, but I cannot decide the headcount alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One wrong allergy tray would stop its live recommendation until the cause was found. A saved hour is not worth putting the wrong food on a cart. I would bring the incident to the safety lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You are eager to pilot it but worried about cuts. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tool will be tested by someone, and I want the counts checked against real trays. I will not hide a useful result to protect a post. I also will not let a speed figure stand in for the whole job.

say: **Steady Disruption** will take routine orders and planning, so I would test a new tool on real routes.
I would count **missed meals and waste** before calling the pilot a saving.
think: A smaller planning office could remove **manager posts**, including mine.
Our **reserve** buys options but cannot decide the company’s staffing choice.
do: **Run** an approved six-week pilot on two routes during 2026.
**Check** automatic changes with the safety lead before live use.
**Apply** for kitchen operations only if salary and morning rota suit the household.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible planning cut despite my tool skills.
S1.quote: A saved hour is not worth putting the wrong food on a cart.
fieldNote: He welcomes an **approved pilot** but measures allergy errors, waste and late carts rather than speed alone.
His **kitchen fallback** needs mortgage pay and a rota compatible with school mornings.

steps.text: Run approved AI pilot on two routes and compare allergy mistakes and waste
Use automatic meal-plan changes only after safety lead checks them
Apply for kitchen lead vacancy only if pay and school-morning rota cover household needs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the office AGI by 2028 could do nearly all the ordering, checking and flight planning we do. We need a date for staffing decisions and a named person who can stop a wrong allergy order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI in 2028 could replace most of my desk work. Robots that can load and prepare meals arrive around 2031, but kitchen-operations planning faces AGI in 2028 too. I expect the planning team to shrink, and my own post might go. A year saved and local jobs give me time to choose, not a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I’d ask the operations director for written cut dates and severance terms. I’d compare three posted food-operations jobs with my current pay and apply only if they include real kitchen checks and a rota my wife and I can manage. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I lose my post, I’d take a confirmed offer only if its pay after travel covers our mortgage and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious rather than stuck. I would be sad to leave a team I built, but we have time to search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a kitchen job stay safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Its schedules and ordering could change in 2028, and capable robots around 2031 could change physical loading and preparation. I would look for a real offer with duties I can do now. I would not sell the children a promise of a permanent safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your wife ask first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the new rota fits her nursing shifts and who has the eight-year-old in the morning. We could pay bills from savings while I searched, but I would not sign a second mortgage on the idea of a new role. We would read the actual contract together.

say: **AGI by 2028** needs cut dates and a person who can stop wrong allergy orders.
I would ask for **severance terms** before any desk closes.
think: Planning work faces AGI in **2028**, before kitchen robots around 2031.
My post might go, but **savings and local jobs** allow a search.
do: **Ask** the director next month for written cut dates and severance.
**Apply** for posted food roles only with real kitchen checks and a workable rota.
**Accept** a confirmed offer after 2028 only if net pay covers mortgage and childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing my team, with room to search.
S2.quote: I would not sell the children a promise of a permanent safe job.
fieldNote: He understands **kitchen paperwork** faces AGI in 2028, while physical preparation changes around 2031.
His **year-long reserve** keeps possible job loss from becoming an immediate bill crisis.

steps.text: Apply for posted food-operations jobs only with kitchen checks and family-compatible rota
Accept confirmed offer after 2028 only if travel-adjusted pay covers mortgage and childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to learn where a kitchen lead still makes decisions when flights change. I would use that time to test the work on site instead of just earning a new badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My planning desk could go in 2031, and a kitchen lead’s ordering and schedules face AGI then too. Robots for hands-on meal work follow around 2034. Five years lets me try a different role while I still have pay, but a real vacancy and a suitable rota are not promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From early 2027 I’d take a paid four-week rotation in the catering kitchen if my director covers the planning desk and keeps my salary. I’d ask the kitchen lead to make me handle one late flight and check my decisions. After 2031 I’d apply for an operations post only if it still has real food-safety work and the pay and family rota fit our mortgage and children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the desk ending, but a rotation could tell me what I need to learn. I would rather find out while still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the late flight test show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I can decide what to remake and what can be kept safely, then get carts to the gate. I know the spreadsheet, not every oven. A kitchen lead would have to correct me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no paid place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current work and ask for one covered kitchen day. I would not take unpaid leave for a trial when the company needs the skill. My wife and I would consider another employer if a real offer appeared.

say: **Five years** allows a paid kitchen rotation before changing roles.
I would test **late-flight decisions** with a kitchen lead.
think: Planning and kitchen schedules face **2031 AGI**, before meal robots around 2034.
A funded rotation and suitable **vacancy** are not guaranteed.
do: **Take** a paid four-week kitchen rotation only with desk cover and full salary.
**Handle** a late-flight food decision with kitchen-lead review during that rotation.
**Apply** after 2031 only for food-safety work with mortgage pay and family rota.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the desk, with time to test kitchen work.
S3.quote: I know the spreadsheet, not every oven.
fieldNote: He names a **food-safety skill gap** despite using AI every day and earning above-average pay.
The **rotation** needs full pay and desk cover; a later vacancy needs mortgage pay and a workable family rota.

steps.text: Take paid four-week kitchen rotation only with planning cover and full salary
Handle late-flight meal decision under kitchen-lead review during paid rotation
Apply after 2031 for food-safety role only with mortgage pay and family rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives the company a decade to show which food-safety jobs remain and what they pay. I would ask for actual vacancies alongside every training offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 our children will be about eighteen and twenty-three. If both wages hold, we could finish more of the mortgage and still keep a strong reserve. My planning and a kitchen lead’s ordering face AGI in 2036, while robots for physical meal work follow around 2039. I would not need to jump at the first opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the kitchen calls and full-pay mortgage overpayments. Each spring I’d review posted food-operations roles and take a paid kitchen assignment only if salary and rota stay workable. After AGI arrives in 2036 I’d remain only while the role has real food-safety duties and enough pay for our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years. A decade and savings let us compare real offers instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put the reserve into your own catering venture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a forecast. I would price equipment, food waste and insurance from a real small contract before risking the household savings. My wife and I prefer one tested step at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real safety duty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need authority to stop a wrong allergy tray before loading and to send back a cart at the wrong temperature. A title that only watches a dashboard would not interest me. I would ask for the duty list in writing.

say: A **decade** should bring posted food-safety jobs and wages.
I would ask for **stop authority** on wrong allergy trays.
think: Both wages could reduce the **mortgage** while preserving a strong reserve.
Planning and kitchen ordering face **2036 AGI**, before meal robots around 2039.
do: **Keep** kitchen calls and full-pay mortgage overpayments in 2026.
**Review** posted food roles each spring; take a paid assignment only with workable salary and family rota.
**Stay** after 2036 only with real food-safety duties and bill-covering pay.
feel: I feel **calm** about the next few years with time and savings.
S4.quote: I would need authority to stop a wrong allergy tray before loading and to send back a cart at the wrong temperature.
fieldNote: His **long runway** lets him demand real safety authority rather than chase a title or speculative venture.
He would price **equipment, waste and insurance** before risking family savings on a business.

steps.text: Continue extra mortgage payments only in full-pay months
Review food roles yearly; take paid assignment only with workable salary and family rota
Stay after 2036 only with food-safety authority and bill-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the planning team could shrink before I have worked enough kitchen shifts to lead there. A written cut date, a paid rotation and a real food-safety vacancy would help. Our savings give us choices, not proof that the next job exists.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who stops an allergy tray when the flight order looks complete. A dashboard can mark a meal loaded while the wrong food sits on the cart. Somebody needs the power to stop it.

headlineQuote: A dashboard can mark a meal loaded while the wrong food sits on the cart.
portrait: **Aaron, 43**, manages airline-catering stock allocation for nine planners and has a bachelor’s degree.
His **high pay**, nurse wife, year-long reserve and many local jobs support a mortgage and two school-age children.
He uses **AI daily** but checks kitchen trays and late flights against people who handle food.
He is **calm** under AI Plateau, anxious about possible 2028 cuts and tests paid kitchen work with safety authority.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink his planning team before he has enough kitchen-lead experience.
whatWouldHelp: A written **cut date**, paid rotation and real food-safety vacancy would help.
